subject: Kemi
title: Laboratory safety and method
sourceSummary: Safety rules and protective equipment in the lab, what the most common hazard pictograms mean, the names and uses of common lab equipment, and how to plan, carry out and document an experiment with a hypothesis and a conclusion.

questions.prompt: What should you always do BEFORE starting an experiment?
questions.opener: It is about knowing what is supposed to happen and what could go wrong.
choices: Taste a little of the substances to find out what they are
Read through the whole instruction and find out what the risks are
Take off your safety goggles so you can see more clearly
Light the burner so it is hot by the time you need it
questions.explanation: By reading the instruction first you know which steps are coming, what protective equipment you need, and what risks the substances carry. Tasting substances in the lab is forbidden - you never know whether a substance is toxic or corrosive.

questions.prompt: What protective equipment do you use when working with chemicals or heating substances?
questions.opener: The eyes are the most sensitive part and the hardest to repair.
choices: Safety goggles and a lab coat or protective apron, and long hair tied back
Just a pair of thin disposable gloves
Ear defenders and a high-visibility vest
No equipment is needed as long as the teacher is in the room
questions.explanation: Safety goggles protect the eyes from splashes, the coat or apron protects clothes and skin, and hair tied back cannot catch fire over the burner. Gloves may sometimes be needed, but they do not protect the eyes - which carry the most serious risk of injury.

questions.prompt: A bottle carries a hazard pictogram showing liquid dripping onto a hand and a surface, corroding them. What does it mean?
questions.opener: Look at what the liquid is doing to the hand in the picture.
choices: Corrosive - can cause serious damage to skin and eyes
questions.explanation: The symbol with liquid corroding a hand and a surface means corrosive, and such substances must be handled with safety goggles and great care. Flammable is instead shown with a flame, and hazardous to the environment with a dead tree and a dead fish.

questions.prompt: You need to measure out exactly 50 ml of water. Which piece of equipment gives the most accurate result?
questions.opener: Some vessels are made for mixing in, others for measuring with.
questions.explanation: The measuring cylinder is narrow and has a clear scale, so you can read off the volume accurately at the bottom of the liquid surface. The markings on a beaker are only approximate - it is made for mixing and pouring, not for measuring precisely.

questions.prompt: The teacher says you may smell the contents of a test tube. How do you do this?
questions.opener: You want a small amount of air to reach your nose, not a large amount.
choices: Put your nose right at the opening and breathe in deeply
Hold the test tube a little way from your face and gently waft the air towards you
Heat the substance first so the smell becomes stronger
Blow into the test tube and smell the air that comes out
questions.explanation: By wafting the air towards you from a distance, you get only a small amount of vapour to your nose, which is safe even if the substance is irritating. Breathing in deeply directly over the opening can damage your airways if the vapour is corrosive or toxic.

questions.opener: It is written before the experiment, not after.
choices: A prediction of what will happen, which can be tested in an experiment
The result you actually measured during the experiment
The conclusion you draw once the experiment is finished
The list of equipment you need
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable guess formulated before the experiment, for example "sugar dissolves faster in warm water". The conclusion comes only afterwards, when you compare the result with the hypothesis and judge whether it was correct.

questions.prompt: You want to investigate whether sugar dissolves faster in warm water than in cold. Describe how you plan, carry out and document the experiment so that the result is reliable.
questions.opener: Think about what you change and what you must keep exactly the same in both trials.
questions.answer: Formulate a hypothesis, change only the temperature and keep everything else the same, time how long it takes to dissolve in both glasses with a stopwatch, write the results in a table, and then compare with the hypothesis in a conclusion.
steps: Write a hypothesis before the trial, for example: "The sugar dissolves faster in the warm water, because the molecules move faster when the temperature is higher."

Decide the variables: what you CHANGE is the temperature of the water (e.g. 10°C and 50°C). Everything else is kept the same - the same volume of water (measured with a measuring cylinder), the same amount of sugar (weighed on a scale), the same stirring.
Carry out the trial: pour the water into two glasses, add the sugar at the same time and start the stopwatch. Stir the same amount in both and stop the clock when the sugar can no longer be seen.
Document: write down the temperature, amounts and measured time in a table. Repeat the trial a couple of times to see whether the result is the same.
Draw a conclusion: compare the times with the hypothesis and state whether it was correct. Also mention anything that could have caused error, for example stirring different amounts in the glasses.

questions.prompt: Summarise the safety rules, the equipment, and the steps in a lab report.
questions.opener: Take safety first, then the equipment, and finally the parts of the report.
questions.answer: Safety rules: read the instruction before you start · never eat, drink or taste anything in the lab · do not run, keep your workspace tidy · keep long hair tied back near an open flame · smell substances by wafting the air towards you from a distance · never pour chemicals back into the original bottle · report spills and accidents to the teacher immediately · wash your hands afterwards · know where the eyewash station, emergency shower, fire extinguisher and fire blanket are · Protective equipment: safety goggles, lab coat or apron, gloves when needed · Hazard pictograms (red frame, white background): flame = flammable · corrosive liquid on a hand = corrosive · skull = acutely toxic · exclamation mark = irritant or harmful to health · dead tree and dead fish = hazardous to the environment · exploding bomb = explosive · Lab equipment: beaker (mixing and pouring, rough volume) · measuring cylinder (measuring volume accurately) · test tube and test tube rack (small amounts, heating) · conical (Erlenmeyer) flask (mixing without spilling) · funnel and filter paper (filtration) · gas burner with tripod and wire gauze (heating) · crucible tongs, scale, thermometer, watch glass · Parts of a lab report: aim · hypothesis (testable prediction made before the trial) · materials and equipment · procedure (clear enough for someone else to repeat it) · results (measurements, table, diagram) · conclusion (was the hypothesis correct, and what sources of error were there?).

questions.prompt: What should you do if you spill a chemical on the lab bench?
questions.opener: Think about who needs to know what happened and can judge whether it's dangerous.
choices: Wipe it up yourself with paper and throw it in the regular bin
Report it to the teacher immediately
Ignore it if it's a small amount
questions.explanation: Spills should always be reported to the teacher immediately, who can judge whether the substance is dangerous and how it should be dealt with properly. Wiping it up yourself and throwing it in the regular bin can be dangerous if the substance is corrosive or toxic.

questions.prompt: Why should long hair be tied back during a lab session?
questions.opener: Think about what's near the bench when something is being heated.
choices: Because it could catch fire near an open flame
Because it gets in the way of your vision
Because it's a school rule with no real reason
questions.explanation: Loose hair can easily catch fire if you lean over an open flame, so it should always be tied back for safety reasons. It's not about appearance, but about avoiding a real fire risk.

questions.prompt: A bottle has a hazard pictogram with a flame on it. What does it mean?
questions.opener: The symbol shows directly what kind of danger is present.
questions.explanation: A flame on the hazard pictogram means flammable — the substance can easily catch fire. Corrosive is instead shown with a liquid corroding a hand and a surface, and toxic with a skull.

questions.prompt: Which equipment is used to heat substances in a test tube?
questions.opener: The equipment produces an open flame.
questions.explanation: The gas burner produces an open flame used to heat test tubes and other containers. A measuring cylinder instead measures volume, and a petri dish and watch glass are used to hold solid samples, not for heating.

questions.prompt: What is the factor you deliberately change in an experiment to see how it affects the result called?
questions.opener: It's the only factor that should differ between the trials.
questions.explanation: The independent variable is what you deliberately change, for example the water's temperature. The dependent variable is instead what you measure as the result, such as the dissolving time.

questions.prompt: You want to investigate whether different amounts of salt affect how quickly ice melts. Describe how you plan, carry out and document the experiment so the result is reliable.
questions.opener: Think about what you change and what you must keep exactly the same in every trial.
questions.answer: Formulate a hypothesis, only change the amount of salt and keep everything else the same, measure the melting time in each trial with a stopwatch, write down the results in a table, and then compare them with the hypothesis in a conclusion.
steps: Write a hypothesis before the trial, for example: "The ice melts faster with more salt, since the salt lowers the ice's freezing point."

Decide the variables: what you CHANGE is the amount of salt (e.g. none, a teaspoon and a tablespoon). Everything else is kept the same — the same amount of ice, the same starting temperature, the same type of container.
Carry out the trial: put equally sized ice cubes in three bowls, add different amounts of salt, and start the stopwatch for all three at the same time.
Document: write down the amount of salt and the melting time for each bowl in a table. Repeat the trial a couple of times to see if the result is the same.
Draw a conclusion: compare the times with the hypothesis and state whether it was correct. Also mention what could have caused errors, for example that the ice cubes weren't exactly the same size.

questions.prompt: A bottle has a hazard pictogram with a skull on it. What does it mean?
questions.opener: The symbol warns of the most serious kind of danger to health.
questions.explanation: The skull means acutely toxic — the substance can cause serious harm or death if inhaled, swallowed or on skin contact. Irritant is instead shown with an exclamation mark, and explosive with an exploding bomb.
